questions.question: Walk me through what happens when an email comes in today.
questions.answer: Whoever's at the counter checks the shared inbox between customers, usually me or Sam. If it's about a repair, we walk to the back and ask the mechanics.

questions.question: How many emails do you get, and what are they about?
questions.answer: About 120 a week. I'd guess more than half are 'is my bike ready yet?' The rest are hours, prices, and the occasional complaint.

questions.question: Where do you keep track of each repair's status?
questions.answer: On a whiteboard in the back. The mechanics update it… usually. Sometimes it's a day behind.

questions.question: What's the most frustrating part of all this?
questions.answer: Every 'is it ready' email means interrupting a mechanic. They hate it, and it slows down repairs. That's honestly what bugs me most.

questions.question: If this were fixed, what would be different?
questions.answer: My mechanics wouldn't get interrupted all day. And customers wouldn't have to email twice because we were slow to answer.

questions.question: Is there anything an answer must never get wrong?
questions.answer: Prices. Last year someone was told $40 for a repair and charged $120. We got a one-star review that still shows up first.

questions.question: What tools do you use, and what's your budget?
questions.answer: We use Square for payments and appointments. I don't want to pay more than about $50 a month for anything new. And nobody here is technical, so it has to be simple.

questions.question: Do you have past emails we could look at?
questions.answer: Sure, everything's in our Gmail going back two years.

questions.question: Which AI model would you like us to use?
questions.answer: I have no idea. Isn't that your job?

questions.question: Would you like the chatbot to have a fun personality?
questions.answer: Sure, I guess? I just want fewer emails.

habits: Ask about the last time, not "usually." Real examples are more accurate than general descriptions.
Get numbers. "A lot of emails" becomes "about 120 a week."
Find where the data lives. An AI tool can only use information that exists somewhere it can reach.
Find who feels the pain. The person who asked isn't always the person most affected.
Hold off on solutions. Once you start pitching, the client stops telling you things.
Summarize it back. "So the main problem is… did I get that right?"
quiz: A client says, "We want a chatbot." What's your first move?
Ask what's happening today that made them want one. Get the last real example, and find out what problem the chatbot is supposed to solve.
The goal is "make reporting faster." What's missing?
A baseline, a target, a way to measure it, and a guardrail. How long does it take now, how fast should it be, where do the numbers come from, and what can't get worse?
Why bother writing down what's out of scope?
It protects your team's time and sets the client's expectations. When a new request comes up mid-project, you can point to what everyone already agreed on.
Discovery shows the data you'd need doesn't exist yet. Now what?
Make getting the data part of the scope, usually the first part. An AI tool can't use information that isn't recorded anywhere, like Copperline's whiteboard.
discovery: Walk me through the last time this happened.
How often does this happen in a week?
How long does each one take?
What does it cost you when it goes wrong?
Where does this information live today?
If this were fixed, what would be different?
What's your budget, and who would maintain this?
